newsitem.title: UK: Soldier hurt in N.Ireland crowd attack.
newsitem.headline: Soldier hurt in N.Ireland crowd attack.

text.p: A soldier was hurt on Wednesday when a mob attacked security forces attempting to clear the main Belfast-to-Dublin railway line of a suspicious object, police said.
Security forces fired plastic bullets to disperse a crowd of about 150 Catholic, Irish nationalist youths in an incident which underlined renewed tension in the British-ruled province.

Police said security forces were first attacked in the afternoon when they tried to clear the railway line at Lurgan, south of Belfast, which has been closed since the weekend because of the suspicious object.
As darkness fell, about 150 youths returned to the scene and threw objects including petrol bombs at police and British troops protecting them.
The injured soldier suffered facial wounds. There were no other reports of injuries and the area was quiet by late evening although the railway line remained closed, police said.

Lurgan, about 30 miles (50 km) south of Belfast, was the scene of a mysterious killing of a taxi driver in July at the height of clashes between pro-British Protestants and security forces over a banned Protestant march.
No group ever claimed responsibility for the killing, but police said it had the hallmarks of pro-British Loyalist guerrillas who fought for 25 years to keep the province British.

Wednesday's Lurgan incident took place three days before a Protestant Order plans to stage a march in Northern Ireland's second city, Londonderry, which was rerouted because of the sectarian violence in July.

Londonderry mayor Richard Dallas vowed he would take part in the Saturday parade despite fears that it might inflame sectarian passions two weeks after IRA guerrillas bombed Britain's main Northern Ireland army base.

Dallas, a member of the pro-British Ulster Unionist Party, said he did not plan to hold negotiations proposed by residents of the Irish nationalist bogside area of Londonderry in a bid to avoid confrontation.
"I think it would be very difficult for the residents to meet with the Apprentice Boys for the sinple reason that there is a lot of mistrust on the Boys side," he said.
Bogside residents objected to the parade, which marks a 17th- century incident when Protestants youths slammed the city's gates shut against an invading Catholic monarch.

Residents say it is intimidation of the Catholic minority by the majority Protestants. The Apprentice Boys say the parade, staged every year for decades, marks a traditional right and has no triumphalist overtones.

The attack by the IRA, which is fighting British rule of Northern Ireland, was the first in the province since the guerrillas called a ceasefire in 1994 which they ended in February this year with bombs outside the province.
